bib.title: A Systematic Survey of Automatic Prompt Optimization Techniques

legacy_report:
SOURCE: A Systematic Survey of Automatic Prompt Optimization Techniques. Ramnath, Zhou, Guan, Mishra, Qi, Shen, Wang, Woo, Jeoung, Wang, Wang, Ding, Lu, Xu, Zhou, Srinivasan, Yan, Chen, Ding, Xu, Cheong (Amazon Web Services). arXiv:2502.16923v2, 2 Apr 2025. Appears to be the EMNLP 2025 version, but the PDF says only "arXiv:2502.16923v2 [cs.CL]". Treat it as a preprint.

COVERAGE: 119,680 of 119,680 chars read, all 31 pages. Main text (about 8 pages) read in full. Appendix read: notation, excluded works, the UCB algorithm, the method-comparison tables, and the prompt examples. The reference list (about chars 30000-77900) and the per-paper task/dataset rows (Tables 5-7) were skimmed only. Tables 2-4 (rows 1-57) were read in part: rows 1-49, 42-49 and the first rows of Table 4. I did not read the rest of rows 50-57 of Table 4 or the dataset columns. Figure captions: only Fig 1 (taxonomy) and Fig 2 (representative APO system).

KEY FACT FOR THE NOTE: this is a pure taxonomy survey. It reports NO experiments and NO benchmark numbers of its own. All figures below are definitions, counts or time costs.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Formal definition of APO. It is a maximisation of expected metric over a validation set for a black-box task model, and it is intractable for discrete token search, so methods approximate it.
  number: none
  setup: Mtask, initial prompt, metric f, eval set Dval.
  quote: "ρopt := arg max ρ∈V Ex∼Dval [f (Mtask(ρ ⊕ x))] (1) This objective function is not tractable for discrete prompt optimization as token-sequence search spaces are combinatorial."
  where: §2, p.1
- APO has three claimed advantages: no parameter access, systematic search, and human-interpretable results.
  number: none
  quote: "(1) they do not require parameter access on LLMs performing the task, (2) they systematically search through the prompt solution space, and (3) they retain human interpretability of prompt improvements."
  where: §1
- Motivation: semantically similar prompts can differ in performance.
  quote: "LLMs still exhibit unpredictable sensitivity to various factors (explanation of the task (Li et al., 2023b),ordering (Liu et al., 2024a), stylistic formatting (Sclar et al.), etc.) causing a performance gap between two prompts that are semantically similar"
  where: §1
- Seed data requirement: a few hundred examples suffice (credited to APE).
  number: "a few hundred samples"
  quote: "APE (Zhou et al., 2022) 1 showed that a few hundred samples are sufficient for further optimization."
  where: §3.1
- Cost of system-prompt optimization versus task-prompt optimization (the only runtime numbers in the survey).
  number: about 60 hours (SPRIG) versus about 10 minutes per task (ProTeGi)
  setup: as stated by the survey; no model or hardware given.
  quote: "optimizing system prompts required a predefined corpus and close to 60 hours whereas Protegi only needed ˜10 minutes per task."
  where: §9.3
- Human preference feedback can improve win rates (Cheng et al. 2024, BPO).
  number: up to 22% for ChatGPT, 10% for GPT-4
  setup: a smaller LLM trained on user preference feedback to rewrite prompts; second-hand, no dataset given.
  quote: "achieving up to 22% increase in win rates for ChatGPT and 10% for GPT-4"
  where: §4.3
- SPRIG's corpus size.
  number: 300 components
  quote: "SPRIG uses a starting corpus of 300 components grouped into categories like COT, roles, styles, emotions, scenarios, and good prop-erties."
  where: §5.1.2
- Vocabulary pruning: CLAPS keeps the top 2000 words nearest cluster centroids.
  number: 2000
  quote: "retain top-2000 words closest to cluster centroids"
  where: §5.1.4
- Self-reflection by an LLM can fail to produce better prompts (Yang et al. 2024b).
  quote: "self-reflection by LLMs can suffer from incorrect error identification, prior biases, semantic invalidity, leading to failure in yielding improved prompts."
  where: §9.2
- Gibberish and "evil twin" prompts can match human ones.
  quote: "prompts have so-called 'evil twins' that are uninterpretable yet recover some of the performance of gold-standard prompts. Lu et al. (2024) showed that rare gibberish strings can serve as competitive delimiters"
  where: §9.2
- Entropy-based and NLL scoring need logprobs, which black-box APIs often do not expose.
  quote: "gradient-free but require access to the entire output probability distribution, something not usually possible with black-box LLMs."
  where: §4.1.3
- LLM feedback adds cost.
  quote: "A potential downside is the inference cost incurred due to an additional LLM call."
  where: §4.2
- Theory: only an upper bound exists.
  quote: "AlignPro (Trivedi et al., 2025) establishes an upper bound on the gains realizable from discrete prompt optimization ... while a lower bound is left unexplored."
  where: §8.1

TAXONOMY (the survey's 5-part framework, Fig. 1 and Algorithm 1)
1. Seed prompts (§3): manual instructions (ProTeGi, GPS, SPRIG); instruction induction by an LLM (Honovich 2023; used by APE, DAPO, MOP, GPO, SCULPT from task READMEs, UniPrompt via filling structured templates).
2. Inference evaluation and feedback (§4):
   - Numeric: task accuracy, reward-model scores (OIRL's XGBoost on query-prompt embeddings, DRPO), entropy-based (CLAPS, GRIPS), and NLL of the output (APE, GPS, PACE).
   - LLM feedback: improving a single candidate (SCULPT, PACE actor-critic, CRISPO multi-aspect critique, AutoHint); improving multiple candidates (ProTeGi and TextGrad "textual gradients", PromptAgent, PREFER, SOS safety, StraGo).
   - Human feedback: GATE, BPO, PROMST, APOHF.
3. Candidate generation (§5):
   - Heuristic edits: Monte Carlo sampling (ProTeGi, PromptAgent MCTS); genetic algorithms (SPRIG, CLAPS token mutation; LLM mutation by LMEA, SOS, StraGo, PromptBreeder, EvoPrompt differential evolution, AELP, GPS, PromptWizard); word/phrase edits (COPLE, GRIPS); vocabulary pruning (CLAPS, BDPL, PIN).
   - Auxiliary trained NN: RL (Prompt-OIRL, BDPL, TEMPERA), fine-tuned LLMs (BPO 7B, FIPO 7B-13B), GAN (Long et al. 2024, Adv-ICL).
   - Metaprompt design (OPRO, PE2, DAPO).
   - Coverage-based: single prompt expansion (AMPO, UniPrompt), mixture of experts (MOP), ensembles (PromptBoosting, Boosted Prompting, PREFER, GPO).
   - Program synthesis (DSP, DSPy, DLN, MIPRO, SAMMO).
4. Filter and retain (§6): TopK greedy; UCB and variants (ProTeGi, SPRIG; UCT for PromptAgent; Linear UCB for AELP); region-based joint search (MOP); metaheuristic ensemble (PLUM: hill climbing, simulated annealing, GA, tabu, harmony).
5. Iteration depth (§7): fixed N steps (most); variable, with a patience parameter (GRIPS) or reward thresholds (PromptAgent: "rt ≤ ϵmin ∨ rt ≥ ϵmax").
Appendix tables 2-4 compare 57 methods on: seed, evaluation, generation, search, depth, time complexity, generation model, target models. Table 1 (main text) compares ProTeGi, APE, CRISPO, MOP, DSPy, OPRO and GATE. In Table 1, OPRO is labelled "Manually created", "Variable", "LLM feedback + Task accuracy", "Metaprompt design", "TopK selection".
Note: the survey's Table 2 gives APE the candidate-generation entry "N/A" or "No new candidates" and "UCB" selection, and DSPy "Program Synthesis" with "TopK selection".

LIMITS
- Authors concede: possible missed papers, forced single-category labels (example: TEMPERA is both RL and phrase-edit), and that the comparison tables had to go to the appendix because of the 8-page limit.
- Scope: black-box discrete prompt optimization only. Excluded (§12.2): FedBPT (soft prompts), Reflexion and Deliberate-then-generate (they do not optimize the input prompt), and AutoPrompt (it needs gradient access). So the note's grouping of AutoPrompt and soft prompts with APE/OPRO is outside this survey's scope.
- It has no head-to-head benchmark comparison and no empirical cost or quality ranking. Complexity columns are asymptotic formulas such as O(N*k*|Dval|*λi), not measurements.
- Open problems the authors list: task-agnostic APO (all methods assume a known task type and, offline, an eval set that production lacks); unclear mechanisms; system prompts and agents (scaling); multimodal APO.
- Dated: it covers work through about early 2025. GEPA, SkillOpt and de Wynter's generalisation result are not in it.
- Mentions TextGrad only as an arXiv preprint (Yuksekgonul et al., 2024), not as Nature 2025.

BUILDS ON: Zhou et al. 2022 (APE); Honovich et al. 2023 (instruction induction); Pryzant et al. 2023 (ProTeGi, textual gradients); Yang et al. 2024a (OPRO); Khattab et al. 2022 and 2024 (DSP, DSPy); Opsahl-Ong et al. 2024 (MIPRO); Fernando et al. 2023 (PromptBreeder); Guo et al. 2024 (EvoPrompt); Wang et al. 2024a (PromptAgent); Zhang et al. 2024b (SPRIG); Wang et al. 2025 (MOP); Yuksekgonul et al. 2024 (TextGrad); Sordoni et al. 2023 (DLN); Schnabel and Neville 2024 (SAMMO); Li et al. 2010 (Linear UCB).

CODE (verbatim, Appendix 14.2, OPRO metaprompt, p. ~30)
"I have some texts along with their corresponding scores. The texts are arranged in ascending order based on their scores, where higher scores indicate better quality. text: Let's figure it out! score: 61 text: Let's solve the problem. score: 63 (. . . more instructions and scores . . . ) ... Write your new text that is different from the old ones and has a score as high as possible. Write the text in square brackets"
Appendix 14.1 (instruction induction): "I gave a friend an instruction and [[n_demo]] inputs. The friend read the instruction and wrote an output for every one of the inputs. Here are the input - output pairs: {{ demos }} What was the instruction ? It has to be less than {{ max_tokens }} tokens ."
Appendix 14.3 gives ProTeGi's "textual gradient" prompt: "I'm trying to write a zero-shot classifier prompt. My current prompt is: "{prompt}" But this prompt gets the following examples wrong: {error_string} give {num_feedbacks} reasons why the prompt could have gotten these examples wrong. Wrap each reason with <START> and <END>".
Appendix 12.3, Algorithm 2 (UCB selection): sample Dsample from Dval, pick the prompt maximizing Q/N + c*sqrt(log t / N), observe reward, update, return the top-B by QT/NT.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.2): taxonomy tree of APO. It shows the five axes and every sub-branch at a glance.
- Fig 2 (p.3): representative APO system. I could not see the picture, and the extraction gives caption text only.
- Algorithm 1 (p.2) is the loop: seed set, Dval, metrics, then generate, select, check convergence, return the argmax. It maps directly onto the note's "The loop" diagram.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions. The extraction is clean text. The tables are flattened but readable, and the reference list is noisy. The survey gives no experimental numbers of its own, so any number the note attributes to APE, OPRO, GEPA and similar comes from the primary papers, not from this one. The word "APE" is disambiguated in a footnote: it means Automatic Prompt Engineer, not "APO".
